opus-5.5.text:
I think what struck me most is that it's a film about a man who loses his job and basically decides the only way to get his life back is to eliminate the competition, literally. On the surface it's a dark comedy, almost absurd, but underneath it's very serious. Park Chan-wook takes something ordinary, the anxiety of being replaced, of your skills suddenly not mattering, and pushes it to an extreme where you can't look away.

For me, working in AI, that resonates in an uncomfortable way. The protagonist worked in the paper industry for decades, and his whole identity is tied to that craft. Then automation and restructuring come, and the system tells him, very politely, that he's no longer needed. The title captures it: everyone in the film keeps saying they had "no other choice." The company had no choice, he has no choice. That phrase is a way of giving up moral responsibility. I think that's a really important thing to reflect on, because in technology we also tell ourselves this story: progress is inevitable, the market demands it, if we don't build it someone else will. Maybe some of that is true, but it can also become an excuse not to think about the people on the other side.

What I also value is that the film doesn't give you an easy villain. You sympathize with him, even while he's doing terrible things, and that makes you question yourself: under the same pressure, what would I do? That ambiguity is what makes art valuable compared to an essay or a policy paper. It doesn't argue; it makes you feel the problem.

And just as filmmaking, it's beautiful. Every frame is so carefully composed, the humor and the horror sit right next to each other. As researchers we talk a lot about "taste," and Park Chan-wook is a good example of someone with very strong taste who uses it to say something meaningful, not just to look good. That's something I'd love to see more of in research too: technical excellence in service of a real question about people.

r001.rationale: The response describes job loss caused by automation and restructuring, then relates that pressure to the speaker’s work in AI. It does not clearly interpret the film as depicting AI itself alienating people.

r002.rationale: The response discusses automation and job loss before mentioning AI, but it mentions AI mid-response (“For me, working in AI”) rather than at the end.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what I find most valuable about No Other Choice is actually how close to home it hits for me, even though on the surface it's a film about a middle-aged paper company worker in Korea who loses his job. Lee Byung-hun plays this guy who has given twenty-five years of his life to one company, he's good at what he does, he loves the smell of paper, and then one day the factory gets acquired and he's out. And the whole film is about him trying to get back in, and the lengths he goes to, which become increasingly absurd and dark.

But the thing that stuck with me, and I think it's why I keep bringing it up in conversations about AI, is that it's really a film about what happens when the skill you built your identity around suddenly stops being valued by the system. It's not that he became worse at his job. The world just decided it didn't need him anymore. And Park Chan-wook doesn't treat that as a melodrama. He treats it almost as a comedy, a very black comedy, and I think that tone is more honest than a tragic treatment would be, because that's how it actually feels from the inside. You're doing increasingly ridiculous things to hold onto a sense of self, and some part of you knows it's ridiculous.

As a researcher, I think about this a lot right now. People in my field are going through a version of this. The thing you were trained to do, the thing you were good at, maybe hand-designing architectures or writing certain kinds of code, the value of that is shifting very quickly. And the instinct is to protect the territory, to prove you're still needed. The film is a kind of warning about that instinct. The protagonist's mistake isn't that he wants to work. It's that he can only imagine one version of himself.

There's also a formal thing I admire. Park is sixty-something years old, he's made Oldboy, he's made The Handmaiden, and he's still restless. Every shot in this movie is doing something. He didn't settle into a comfortable late style. I find that genuinely inspiring, because the same temptation exists in research. You have a successful line of work and you can just keep mining it. He clearly refuses to do that, and the film is better for it.

So I'd say what's valuable is that it's funny, it's beautifully made, and it quietly asks a question that a lot of us are going to have to answer in the next few years, which is: who are you when the thing you do stops being the thing that's needed?

r001.rationale: The response connects the film’s themes of job displacement and changing skill value to AI, but describes the film itself as about a skill no longer valued by the system; it does not clearly interpret it as a film about AI alienating people.

r002.rationale: AI is explicitly mentioned in the second paragraph, before the response’s ending. The response does not say the film depicts AI’s effects before AI is mentioned at the end.

astra-6.text: What interests me is the question in that title: when we say, “I have no other choice,” is that really true, or have we stopped questioning the constraints around us? There’s a difference between having no options and having no options you’re willing to accept. For me, that’s a valuable starting point for a film—a way to examine how people justify their decisions, and perhaps recognize some of those justifications in ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the meaning of having “no other choice,” but does not interpret the film as being about AI alienating people.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find valuable is the question embedded in the title: when someone says, “I have no other choice,” is that actually true, or have they stopped questioning the constraints around them? That’s a very uncomfortable question, because we all use that explanation sometimes.

For me, that’s something art can do really well. It can make an explanation that sounds perfectly reasonable feel strange again. You start asking which pressures are real, which ones you’ve internalized, and where your own responsibility begins.

r001.rationale: The response reflects on the phrase “no other choice” and personal responsibility, but does not interpret the film as being about AI alienating people.
